fields.title: Promises no one ever made
fields.keyTakeaway: Everything consumers start relying on becomes an obligation regardless of agreements, and the only defense is to explicitly and preemptively state what is not guaranteed.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A partner built a workflow on a field we considered internal. Are we obligated to maintain it?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A product gradually accumulates obligations no one ever accepted. Every field, every format, every behavior someone starts relying on becomes a de facto promise. After a few years, change freedom disappears, and no one can name the moment it happened.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[backward-compatibility|Backward compatibility]] is a new version's ability to work with old clients. The obligation to maintain it arises in two ways.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: *Explicitly.* Written in a contract or policy: these operations are stable, breaking changes in 6 months.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: *Implicitly.* No one promised anything, but consumers rely on it, and breaking it means losing their trust. This works as an obligation regardless of formalities.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Implicit obligations pop up where you least expect them:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *Element order in lists,* which you didn't guarantee, but someone relies on it. *Identifier format.* You wrote "string," output numbers — someone parses it as a number. *Error messages.* Text is parsed by code because the error code wasn't specific enough. *Timings.* "Usually arrives in a second" becomes an expectation. *Side effects.* An operation does something extra besides its main job, and people rely on it.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: The defense is **explicit limitation of what is promised.** The contract states not only what is guaranteed, but also what is not: order is undefined, identifier format is opaque, error text may change, error codes will not.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: This is cheap at the start and nearly impossible to introduce later. Declaring "order was never guaranteed" after three years of stable ordering is formally true and practically useless.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: The second tool is **measurement.** An obligation arises when someone relies on something; knowing who relies on what is only possible via usage logs.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Position order in an order.* Never guaranteed, happened to match addition order. Query optimization changed it, and three partners got discrepancies in pick lists — their systems relied on the order. Reverted by adding explicit sorting and writing it into the contract.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Error text on product unavailability.* An integrator from one chain parsed it as a string because error code `409` was shared across several cases. Changing the wording broke their parsing. The right takeaway is not "their fault," but "error codes were insufficiently detailed": we added subcodes.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Webhook delay.* Usually a second. One chain built a workflow on the assumption that a webhook would arrive within five seconds. When things slowed down, their workflow broke. Here we refused: timing was never promised, and we are not ready to promise it. But we added an explicit caveat to the documentation that wasn't there before.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The team's general takeaway: **if consumers rely on undescribed behavior, it's usually a documentation flaw rather than their fault.**
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Absolute compatibility is impossible and unnecessary. The goal is to consciously choose what is promised rather than discovering it by accident.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Everything consumers begin to rely on becomes an obligation regardless of agreements, and the only protection is to explicitly state in advance what is not guaranteed.
